Anthropic orders AI tool Claude to stop remaking video games
Update: Anthropic has confirmed it's released an update to Opus 5.5 to "steer" Claude Code away from "recreating someone else's specific game."
Bryant Francis
,
Senior Editor
,
GameDeveloper.com
October 30, 2026
schedule
2 Min Read
Image via Anthropic
It appears
Anthropic
may be (quietly) taking action to stem the flood of AI-driven game remakes that have hit the video game industry in the last few month, which saw users creating their own versions of classic and upcoming games, sometimes for fun, sometimes for financial gain.
Earlier today X (formerly Twitter) user
Chasm
said that they spotted an update to Claude Code's "rules" that was pushed sometime on October 27. The rule is listed under "tengu_heron_brook," and reads "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Do not build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original." Chasm reports that there is no way to disable the rule.
An Anthropic spokesperson referred us to a statement by Anthropic member of technical staff Addy Osmani also posted on X. "We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy," Osmani wrote. "Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance."

"In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way."
Fear over the potential of fast-follow AI remakes that might beat the copied game to market has spread among independent developers in the last few weeks. Digital Sun Games is one of
several studios
to
cancel their upcoming public playtest
for fear someone might ingest the demo into an AI tool and release their own version of its upcoming game
ReVamp
. Developers have also pressed Valve to explain how it can prevent the shady clones from supplanting their games on Steam, prompting the company to offer a rare explanation to developers in South Korea
earlier in this week
.
While developers may take some relief that Anthropic at least doesn't want to actively encourage mass game copying, this rule may only deter the most low-effort copycats.
Scientists
and reporters have
repeatedly documented
that safety limits on generative AI tools can be sidestepped by deploying
rhetorical tricks
. It's also unclear how the software would be able to interpret whether or not a user owns a game idea or game assets.
And as many users responding to Chasm pointed out, if Claude becomes too difficult to use, vibe-coding cloners can turn to open-weight models that
have no such restrictions in place.
GameDeveloper.com has reached out to Anthropic for comment and will update this story upon its response.

This story has been updated with confirmation from Anthropic.
